title: Concepts of Programming Languages
summary: How programming language features work, learnt by building them: each week you extend a definitional interpreter in Scala for a small teaching language called Paret, adding functions, scoping, mutation, types, objects and laziness. Lectures also cover parallel programming with OpenMP and concurrency abstractions such as locks, STM and futures. The weekly WebLab interpreter assignments are a pass/fail requirement, and the grade comes entirely from one computer exam in WebLab.

basis.description: Slides of Lectures 2 to 15 of CSE2120 (2024-25) as text, the WebLab exercises and Cementing tasks, and seven past WebLab exams. Lecture 1 (motivation and organisation) and the Course Recap, which has no slide text, are not counted. Time shares count content slides, with repeated animation frames counted once.
basis.caveat: The material is from CSE2120, the old code. From 2026-27 the course is CSE22C and runs in quarter 2 instead of quarter 3; the content is said to be unchanged. Slide counts understate laziness: its deck is short, yet it is examined in every paper. The scoping share is inflated by long step-by-step environment animations, and Lecture 3 holds two near-identical decks, counted once.

topics.name: Syntax, parsing and abstract syntax
know: Concrete syntax (the program text) versus [[abstract syntax (the tree that keeps only the structure)]], and what a parser does between them
Grammars in BNF and in the SDF context-free syntax notation used for Paret, where each production names the AST constructor it builds
Ambiguity and how [[priorities and associativity]] remove it
Algebraic data types in Scala: [[sealed abstract classes and case classes]] as an inductive definition of the AST
Pattern matching in Scala: literals, wildcards, variables, guards, list patterns and nested patterns
do: Decide whether a program parses under a given grammar and, if it does, write its AST in flat constructor form
Explain why a program fails to parse, naming the production that is missing or ambiguous
Define case classes for a small grammar and write a parser or recursive function over them
pitfalls: Reading a grammar too loosely: check exactly how identifiers, literals and separators are defined before deciding that a program parses
Old exams write Paret with parentheses (S-expressions); the course now uses a different surface syntax for the same structures

topics.name: Semantics, interpreters and desugaring
know: Static versus dynamic semantics, and [[operational, denotational and axiomatic]] ways of giving meaning
Big-step semantics: reading inference rules of the form [[environment, expression evaluates to value]]
The pipeline [[parse, desugar into a small core language, then interpret into values]] (NumV, BoolV, closures)
Interpretation versus compilation
Desugaring: rewriting extended syntax (and, or, multi-armed conditionals) into core syntax, and why that keeps the interpreter small
Short-circuit evaluation and the laws that and and or must satisfy
The lab's style rules: [[structural recursion, no for or var]]
do: Write the interp function in Scala by pattern matching on the core AST, throwing the right exception on errors
Write a desugar function that maps every extended construct to core syntax, recursively
Evaluate a program by hand with given big-step rules and spot which rule makes the result differ from the lab
pitfalls: Using non-structural (generative) recursion; the exam deducts points for it

topics.name: Higher-order functions and currying
know: Functions as values: lambdas, anonymous functions, and functions that take or return functions
map, filter and fold, and how they differ
Scala functions: def versus val, function types such as [[Int => Int => Int]], functions inside functions
Currying and partial application, and three ways to curry a function in Scala
How objects can emulate lambdas (Java functional interfaces) and how lambdas can emulate objects
do: Recognise whether a given recursive function over a tree or list is a map, a fold or something else
Translate between a Java method or JavaScript function and a Paret lambda
Write a desugarer that turns multi-argument functions and applications into curried single-argument ones
pitfalls: Calling something a fold when no accumulator is threaded through; [[applying a function to each element on its own is a map]]

topics.name: Substitution, environments and scoping
know: Substitution-based evaluation of let and lambda, free and bound variables, name shadowing and name capture
Environments as delayed substitution: [[a list of bindings from names to values]]
Closures ([[ClosV with parameters, body and the defining environment]]) and why lexical scoping needs them
Static (lexical) versus dynamic scoping, and that [[let behaves like applying a lambda]]
Laws of a language, such as beta reduction, and checking an interpreter against them
Recursion without built-in recursion: passing the function to itself, and fixed-point combinators such as Z
do: Evaluate a program under static and under dynamic scoping and give both results
Trace an environment-based interpreter step by step, writing the environment at each subexpression
Implement functions, let-bound functions and pattern matching in an environment-based interpreter
Rewrite a recursive program so it works without letrec
pitfalls: Evaluating a function body in [[the caller's environment]] instead of the closure's environment: that gives [[dynamic scoping]]
Assuming name capture cannot happen in a substitution interpreter; any construct that binds names can cause it

topics.name: Mutation, state and memory
know: Boxes ([[box, unbox, set-box]]) as first-class memory locations, versus mutable variables with assignment and seq
The store-passing interpreter: [[the environment maps names to locations, the store maps locations to values]], and every interp call returns a value and a new store
letrec with a store: [[bind the names to placeholder locations first, then fill them]]
Pass-by-value versus pass-by-reference
Side effects, evaluation order, and pure versus impure languages
Garbage collection: [[mark-and-sweep, reference counting, copying collectors]], and Rust ownership and borrowing as an alternative
do: Predict the result of a program with mutation, stating which store each step sees
Implement variables, assignment, while loops or a pass-by-reference operator in a store-passing interpreter
Desugar sequencing or loops into core constructs that use the store
pitfalls: Expecting a callee's assignment to its parameter to change the caller's variable under pass-by-value

topics.name: Type checking and type inference
know: Type safety and the slogan that [[well-typed programs cannot go wrong]]; static versus dynamic checks
A type checker as a function typeOf from expression and type environment to type, and the typing rules behind it
Typing lambdas, applications, lists and letrec, and why [[letrec needs annotations while let does not]]
Parametric polymorphism, and what cannot be typed without it
Type inference by [[generating constraints with type variables and solving them by unification]]; let polymorphism
Subtyping (records, function types), union and intersection types, nullability and dependent types
do: Decide whether a program type checks, and whether a type-safe program can still fail at run time
Implement typeOf for new constructs (records, named arguments, parity of numbers, nullable types)
Infer the type of a small expression by writing and unifying its constraints
pitfalls: Mixing up a program that fails to type check with one that type checks but crashes at run time; multiple-choice questions turn on this difference

topics.name: Parallel programming
know: Task, data and pipelined parallelism
OpenMP: parallel regions, [[parallel for, critical, barriers, nowait, private, shared and firstprivate]] variables
Static versus dynamic loop scheduling
[[Speedup, efficiency and Amdahl's law]], and its limits
Data dependences ([[true, anti and output]]) and loop-carried dependences after loop normalisation
do: Decide whether a loop can be parallelised and add the right OpenMP pragma
Compute speedup, efficiency or the Amdahl bound for a given serial fraction and core count
Find the dependences in a loop and say which iterations conflict
pitfalls: Parallelising a loop that has a loop-carried dependence, which changes its result

topics.name: Concurrency
know: Concurrency versus parallelism, threads and preemption
[[Race conditions, deadlock, starvation, fairness and Heisenbugs]], with dining philosophers as the example
Critical sections and locks, and the problems locks bring
Atomic read-modify-write operations such as Java's AtomicInteger
Software transactional memory (transactions, retry, composition), futures and promises, async/await and coroutines
Avoiding races by design: Rust's ownership rules and pure languages
do: Judge whether a given Java class is safe under concurrent use and name the interleaving that breaks it
Fix an unsafe class with a lock, synchronized or an atomic type
Write a short sequence of calls that triggers the failure
pitfalls: Saying code is unsafe without [[naming the non-atomic step or the interleaving]]; model answers require it

topics.name: Objects
know: The functional versus object-oriented way of splitting operations and data variants
Classes, constructors, self, inheritance and subtyping in Scala
Late binding of self and dynamic dispatch
Delegation and message forwarding, and JavaScript's prototype delegation
Objects as functions with state, and desugaring classes or objects into lambdas and records
How objects are laid out in memory: stack versus heap
do: Evaluate a program with objects, delegation and late binding of self
Implement objects with fields and methods in an interpreter, or desugar classes into core syntax
pitfalls: Looking up a method or field in the parent when [[late binding means self still refers to the child object]]
There is no mandatory lab assignment on objects, yet it is exam material

topics.name: Lazy evaluation
know: Call-by-value, call-by-name and call-by-need
Thunks: [[a suspended expression with its environment]]
Strictness points: [[places such as arithmetic and conditions that force a thunk]]
Memoisation in call-by-need: [[a thunk is evaluated at most once]]
Infinite lazy lists in Scala and in Paret
do: Count how many times an argument is evaluated under each strategy
Implement call-by-name or call-by-need in an interpreter with thunks and a strict function
Desugar a lazy list construct into core syntax
pitfalls: Forgetting to force a thunk at a strictness point, so a thunk value leaks into arithmetic
Counting evaluations under call-by-need as if it were call-by-name

prerequisites: Object-oriented programming in Java (Introduction to Programming)
Testing your code and writing readable, maintainable code (Software Quality and Testing)
practical: Every week a mandatory WebLab assignment extends a Paret interpreter in Scala: arithmetic, functions and environments, mutation with a store, type checking and more. You may resubmit as often as you like before the lab deadline, with automatic feedback; if all but one are passed you can request a repair with extra work. The lab is pass/fail and individual. Optional exercises are marked Basis, Exam Level or Extra, and the Wednesday Cementing sessions give one larger task a week.
studyAdvice: Do the mandatory interpreter assignments yourself and properly: about three quarters of the exam points are for Scala code of the same kind, in the same WebLab setting.
Get closures, environments and the store right first. Scoping, mutation, laziness and objects all build on the same interpreter, and together they carry most exam points.
Practise writing type checkers: one programming question per paper is a type checker for a new construct.
Work the Exam Level exercises on WebLab; recent papers reuse their themes (currying, recursion without recursion, safety of concurrent classes).
Revise parallel programming and concurrency for the theory part: both 2025 papers had three-part questions on each.
Sit at least two past papers in WebLab under exam conditions, three hours and only the Scala API, and keep to functional style throughout.
